extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, journalists, media scholars, and interested general readers
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing news with the propaganda model
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Chomsky and Herman's propaganda model to evaluate how structural and economic forces shape news content; identify which filters (ownership, advertising, sourcing, flak, common enemy) are operating and how they affect selection, framing, and omission. Useful for media criticism, newsroom self-reflection, and teaching critical news literacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: The propaganda model (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: A framework built around five structural filters through which news must pass; information that serves dominant interests moves through easily while information that challenges them is blocked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of the five filters as layers shaping which stories become news: selection, framing, and omission produce outcomes that appear objective while upholding the ideological status quo. The model emphasises systemic, institutional causes of bias rather than individual malice. Use the model as an analytical lens to trace how economic and structural logic produces patterned outcomes across outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 1: ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns the size, concentrated ownership, owner wealth, and profit orientation of dominant media corporations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large media organisations are often subsidiaries of larger conglomerates; their fundamental obligation to shareholders and profit can push editorial decisions away from journalism that threatens owners or business partners. Expect homogenisation of perspectives and constrained debate when ownership is concentrated. Evidence to look for: cross-ownership links, corporate parent interests, coordinated editorial positions across outlets owned by the same conglomerate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 2: advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising revenue as the primary financial support for media, making advertisers effectively the media's real customer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because audiences rarely cover full costs, advertisers fill revenue gaps; this shapes editorial choices because aggressive reporting about an advertiser's industry risks lost revenue. The effect can be conscious or tacit (professional culture). When evaluating coverage, consider advertiser exposure, native advertising, and whether reporting avoids or softens stories that could threaten major advertisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 3: sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Where news organisations obtain information: concentrated resources at key 'terminals' such as government press offices, corporate PR, and industry-funded think tanks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large outlets rely on low-cost, reliable flows of content from official sources, producing a symbiotic relationship where government and corporate spokespersons become default authoritative voices. This biases coverage toward official narratives and raises the barrier for civil society, whistleblowers, and independent researchers. Evaluate whose voices are amplified and whether independent sources have meaningful access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 4: flak
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative feedback directed at media organisations (organised campaigns, legal threats, political pressure, expensive lawsuits) intended to punish or intimidate critical coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flak can be costly even when not legally successful; organisations may self-censor to avoid resource-draining responses. Look for patterns where outlets avoid topics that historically produced intense pushback or where editorial decisions reflect a risk-avoidant posture. Examples: industry-funded campaigns attacking scientists, strategic lawsuits to intimidate outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 5: the common enemy
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of a shared national or societal enemy (originally anticommunism) to rally public opinion and marginalise dissent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The shared enemy creates an 'us versus them' framing that delegitimises critics and narrows permissible debate. Though the specific enemy changes over time (e.g., terrorism, immigration, socialism), its function is to frame difficult questions as disloyal or dangerous. When analysing coverage, note whether dissenting voices are portrayed as unpatriotic or extreme rather than engaged on substantive grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias as structural, not conspiratorial (not a conspiracy theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: The model emphasises that elite domination of media and marginalisation of dissent occurs 'so naturally' within institutional structures that journalists can act in good faith while producing biased outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid interpreting patterns as evidence of coordinated orders from a central authority; instead trace incentives, organisational rules, and routine practices that lead to systematic selection and framing. This reframing helps identify institutional reforms rather than seeking individual conspirators.

rubrics_metrics.name: How the filters map onto the digital/platform era
rubrics_metrics.description: The original filters persist but have migrated: platform ownership concentrates gatekeeping (Google, Meta, Amazon); advertising operates through surveillance capitalism; algorithms elevate ‘authoritative’ sources; flak becomes coordinated online harassment, demonetisation, and platform suppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying the model to contemporary media, examine platform control of distribution, data-driven ad incentives, algorithmic amplification of certain sources, and new forms of flak (deplatforming, mass reporting, monetisation strikes). Look for structural parallels rather than assuming the internet has eliminated the filters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known critiques and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars argue the model can be overly deterministic, totalising, and US-centric; it may understate genuine journalistic resistance and differences between outlets. Chomsky and Herman acknowledged the filters do not eliminate all critical journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the model as a heuristic, not an iron law. Assess cross-national applicability, variation across outlet types (independent vs corporate), and empirical evidence of adversarial journalism. Be cautious about overstating uniformity and allow for exceptions and temporal change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic implications and critical news consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: If mass media are structurally shaped to serve elite interests, democratic participation can become ritualised; citizens debate within frameworks set by media systems they did not design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practical takeaway is to 'read the news critically'—notice not just what is reported but what is omitted, whose voices are treated as credible, and which questions are never seriously asked. Apply the filters diagnostically to assess how media structure conditions democratic discourse and to identify possible sites for reform or alternative information practices.
